# The Beam: how laser shows work - the planetarium years, the machines, the rules

> An independent, cited guide to laser light shows: how a beam becomes a picture, Laserium and the planetarium era, gas tubes to diodes, how shows are programmed, why lasers can injure and who regulates them, and what a show costs.

Independent cited field guide, 34,734 words, 285 sources, updated November 2026. Not affiliated with any manufacturer, software maker, show company, venue, artist or agency. General information, not safety or legal advice.

## Sections
- [What a laser show is](https://beam.cold.fyi/basics/): A laser show is a narrow beam of colored light, steered by two small mirrors fast enough that your eye reads the moving dot as lines, fans, tunnels or cartoons. In the air it needs haze to be seen at all; on a wall it draws like a pen. Plenty of things with "laser" on the box are something else - video projectors, star projectors, searchlights, stage "holograms" - and the difference comes down to whether a raw beam leaves the machine.
- [A history of the laser show, 1960 to 2000](https://beam.cold.fyi/history/): The first laser fired in 1960, but it only flashed red; shows needed the steady, colored beams of the argon and krypton gas lasers that arrived in 1964. Artists were bending those beams through fog by the late 1960s, a composer and a physicist scanned them to music in 1969, and Laserium made the idea a ticketed night out in 1973. Rock tours picked lasers up in 1975, US regulators were at the shows by 1978, and by the late 1990s the hand-played analog console had mostly given way to a computer.
- [The planetarium laser show: Laserium, Laser Floyd and why it never died](https://beam.cold.fyi/planetarium/): The planetarium laser show began on November 19, 1973, when Ivan Dryer's Laserium opened at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles with one krypton laser and a person playing it live to recorded music. It spread to dozens of cities, turned into the rock-album format of Laser Floyd and Laser Zeppelin, lost its home dome in 2002 and kept going anyway. The shows running now are mostly supplied by a few companies, the projectors are digital, and the album might be Taylor Swift's, but the idea is the one Dryer sold in 1973.
- [The lasers: from gas tubes to diodes](https://beam.cold.fyi/lasers/): For roughly 30 years a professional laser show meant a tube of ionized argon or krypton that could pull tens of kilowatts from three-phase power, drank gallons of cooling water a minute and gave back well under a tenth of a percent of that energy as light. Green solid-state lasers arrived in the late 1990s, direct diodes took over blue and then green by 2013, and by 2004 a 5 W full-color laser could already run from a standard outlet. Watts are only part of brightness - divergence and wavelength decide what the eye sees - and in the US, federal law lists the safety hardware every Class IIIb and IV projector has to carry.
- [Steering the beam: scanners, color and effects](https://beam.cold.fyi/scanning/): A laser show picture is one dot, moved so fast by two small mirrors that the eye joins it into lines. The mirrors ride on galvanometers rated in points per second, and "30K at 8 degrees" means the pair can draw ILDA's standard test pattern correctly at 30,000 points per second when the pattern is 8 degrees wide. Color comes from switching and dimming the lasers themselves, a job a crystal modulator did in the gas era, and a good share of classic effects never touch a scanner at all.
- [Programming and running a show](https://beam.cold.fyi/programming/): A laser image is a list of points that two mirrors chase tens of thousands of times a second, with the beam switched off between shapes. Software arranges those points into cues or a timeline, a converter box turns them into voltages, and a trained operator stays at the controls with an emergency stop in reach. Most of the vocabulary a newcomer meets - ILDA cable, test pattern, zones, timecode, busking - names one link in that chain.
- [Why lasers can hurt you, and how shows are made safe](https://beam.cold.fyi/safety/): A visible laser beam passes through the front of the eye and is focused onto the retina, so a few milliwatts in the wrong place can do damage that a far brighter lamp cannot. The exposure limit for a visible beam assumes a blink or a turned head within a quarter of a second, and it works out to about 2.5 mW/cm2. Show safety is the work of keeping every beam a person could meet under that limit - with distance, a wider beam, a moving beam and a fast cutoff when something fails.
- [The rules: who regulates laser shows, country by country](https://beam.cold.fyi/rules/): In the United States a show laser above 5 mW of visible output is lawful only under a variance from the FDA, and a beam that leaves for open sky brings in the FAA. Most other countries have no laser show license at all: general workplace safety law and the same [exposure limit](/safety/) apply, and guidance documents carry the practical detail. Past the US, UK, Germany, Canada and Australia, the country-by-country picture comes from a list the trade association itself calls unofficial.
- [On stage: tours, festivals, companies and costs](https://beam.cold.fyi/stage/): Pink Floyd's 1994 US tour carried two 50 W laser systems; by 2025 the Guinness record stood at 1,100 separate laser sources in one stadium. The same short list of specialist companies turns up in the credits, and they publish gear lists far more readily than prices. Ticket prices, a US paperwork fee of zero and a few manufacturer list prices are public. Day rates, insurance and the size of the whole business are not.
- [Laser shows now: cheap diodes, fireworks and what is next](https://beam.cold.fyi/now/): Between about 2005 and 2014 the laser show moved off water-cooled gas tubes and onto solid-state and then diode sources, and rigs went from a pair of lasers to hundreds. Cities have begun using lasers and drones where fireworks used to go, mostly for reasons of fire, smoke and noise. The rules for buying and running a show laser have barely moved: in the US, anything above 5 mW of visible output still needs an FDA variance, and the regulator keeps a standing import alert on projectors that arrive without one.
- [Test yourself, and where to dig next](https://beam.cold.fyi/next/): A quiz on everything above, the dates in order, the landmark shows, the vocabulary, the best places to keep reading, and the questions nobody has answered in public yet.
